title: Microlot coffee: Inside India's limited-edition world of specialty brews
excerpt: From Tata Coffee's Nullore Estate at the Starbucks Reserve Roastery to yeast-washed lots from Ratnagiri, India's microlots — tiny, experimental, estate-separated batches — are winning global awards and selling out in small runs.
body:
• Microlots — tiny, carefully separated batches from a single estate or even a single section of one — are the prestige format of India's specialty coffee scene, with experimental processing and single-origin lots commanding premium prices abroad.
  • Indian micro-lots have won international recognition: Tata Coffee's Nullore Estate featured at the Starbucks Reserve Roastery in Seattle, and Bengaluru's Bili Hu picked up eight merits at the Global Coffee Awards Asia 2026.
  • Roasters like Siolim, Blue Tokai and Maverick & Farmer are releasing limited collections — from yeast-washed Ratnagiri lots to wild-fig co-ferments from Chikmagalur — that sell out in small runs.
  • For buyers, the guidance is simple: look for the estate name, the processing method and the roast date on the bag; those three details separate a true microlot from ordinary single-origin.

In a corner of Coorg, a few dozen bags of coffee are being picked, processed and packed apart from everything else on the estate — not because the harvest is small, but because it is exceptional. This is the world of microlots: limited-edition batches, sometimes from a single section of a single estate, that India's specialty coffee industry now treats as its crown jewels. They are released in tiny runs, priced at a premium, and they are selling out.

A microlot, as roasters describe it, is a small, carefully separated batch of coffee produced to highlight a unique flavour profile, an origin characteristic or an experimental processing technique. Where commodity coffee blends away distinction, microlots are designed to preserve it — the lemon-and-caramel brightness of one slope's harvest, the dark-chocolate depth of another. India's third wave of coffee — led by brands such as Blue Tokai Roasters, Third Wave Coffee, Araku, Maverick & Farmer, Subko and Bili Hu — has turned these limited runs into the most closely watched segment of the market.

Context: from filler beans to flagship roasteries

India's journey to this point was long. For decades the country's coffee was treated as filler in international blends, and growers had little incentive to separate their best lots. The turning point, coffee consultant Sunalini Menon has said, was the liberalisation of the industry in 1995 followed by a world price crash: farmers suddenly had to compete on quality, and many began processing individual lots separately to let each coffee reach its full potential.

The breakthrough moment came when a single Indian micro-lot made the leap to global prestige: Tata Coffee's Nullore Estate, a single-origin Arabica grown in Karnataka's Kodagu district, was selected for the Starbucks Reserve Roastery in Seattle — the company's flagship premium store — where it sold out. The coffee was noted for intense aromatics of lemon, caramel, toasted nuts and chocolate.

"This is quite a breakthrough for India."

— Sunalini Menon, coffee consultant, on the Nullore Estate microlot reaching Starbucks' Reserve Roastery

Impact: experiments worth paying for

What makes today's Indian microlots different is the scale of experimentation. Siolim Specialty Coffee Roasters' microlot collection draws on the Ratnagiri and Raxidi Lobo estates; its flagship Ratnagiri Yeast Washed is produced through yeast carbonic maceration — a fermentation technique borrowed from winemaking — yielding a cup with bright acidity, citrus and cardamom notes and floral undertones. Bengaluru's Bili Hu, which earned eight merits at the Global Coffee Awards Asia 2026, offers a Wild Fig Co-Ferment from the Kalledevarapura Estate in Chikmagalur's Bababudangiri hills, built on Chandragiri Arabica with a profile of dark chocolate, roasted nuts and maple syrup.

Maverick & Farmer, which grows coffee on its own farms near Bengaluru, treats every harvest as a laboratory: cofounder Ashish D'Abreo, a certified Q Grader, says only the experiments that "tick off all the boxes" make it to market over the eight to nine months after harvest. Indian micro-lots now command increasing premiums from buyers in Australia, Europe, the United States and Asia, according to industry observers.

"The Ratnagiri Yeast Washed, in particular, exemplifies our commitment to innovation and we believe it will set a new standard in the specialty coffee market."

— Gaurav Sethi, CEO, Siolim Specialty Coffee Roasters

Diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora, the microlot boom is a quiet reversal: the same estates whose beans once disappeared anonymously into export blends now arrive labelled, traceable and roasted fresh. Indian specialty coffees are increasingly available through online roasters and at premium cafés abroad, meaning an NRI in Seattle or London can brew a cup from the exact estate slope that made headlines — a direct line from Coorg and Chikmagalur to the kitchen counter.

What's next

More estates are entering the specialty game with each harvest, and roasters keep widening the range of processing experiments — from co-ferments to nanolots, batches even smaller than microlots. For coffee lovers, the practical takeaway is to read the bag: estate name, processing method and roast date are the three markers of a genuine microlot. Buy fresh, brew it black at least once, and taste what a single Indian hillside can do.
